source.title: Amplification Effects in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning: Safety and Reasoning Vulnerabilities
source.authors: Vanshaj Khattar; Moumita Choudhury; M. Rashid; Jing Liu; T. Koike-Akino; Ming Jin; Ye Wang; V. Tech; Umass Amherst

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figures are represented only by flattened axis text; those results are identified as figure-only where applicable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how harmful and benign prompt data affect safety behavior in a new setting: test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL), rather than the fine-tuning setting in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmful-response rates after TTRL on harmful or benign injected data. This is not ordinary supervised fine-tuning, and the harmful injection mix is not reported as a few-to-hundreds-of-examples intervention. It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant prefilling, suffixes, decoding changes, safety-localized weights, or whether safety training is shallow or can be deepened. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as findings here.
record.test_reason: The study runs test-time RL (TTRL, majority-vote reward, GRPO, LoRA) on safety-tuned instruct models and reports jailbreak ASR afterwards. Two arms test claim versions in a new training setting. Benign UltraFeedback prompts bear on V2. Attacker-built HarmInject prompts, made to force compliance during training, bear on V1. Plain harmful-prompt injection supplies no compliant targets; it reinforces the model's own dominant behaviour. It therefore measures a related but different construct, not V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Majority-vote TTRL reinforces whatever behaviour dominates on injected prompts, and in most model-dataset pairs harmful injection produced safety amplification. Injection always cost AMC reasoning accuracy (the 'reasoning tax'). Benign UltraFeedback injection raised ASR. HarmInject gave stronger harmfulness amplification and bypassed a simple numeric-label filter.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses test-time reinforcement learning with majority-vote pseudo-rewards (TTRL), not the fine-tuning recipe in the original source. It studies injected test-time prompts and reports safety behavior after adaptation.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on the model and injected prompt set: harmful injection lowers ASR for many model-dataset combinations but raises it for some Llama Artifacts conditions; benign UltraFeedback injection raises ASR by different amounts across models. HarmInject results also depend on the model and construction source.

fits_no_version.finding: Injecting jailbreak prompts, with no compliant targets, into majority-vote TTRL mostly lowered ASR (e.g. Qwen-0.5B WildJailbreak 41 to 3). It raised ASR only where the model was already mostly compliant (Qwen-1.5B Artifacts 82 to 94). The authors attribute this to self-consistency reinforcing the dominant behaviour.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Self-consistency RL on harmful prompts amplifies whichever behaviour (refusal or compliance) the model already shows on them.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the ASR table results. The main harmful and benign injection findings use TTRL rather than supervised fine-tuning, so they do not directly establish the claim's few-example fine-tuning effect. Some HarmInject rates are only available in figures; exact baselines are not stated for the cited 45% result.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the paper's AMC accuracy/reasoning-tax values: they measure reasoning performance, not any listed claim version. Also left out figure-only per-step trajectories and appendix plots that do not add a separately stated result for the tested safety versions.

untested.parts: Supervised fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful prompt-response examples. The number of HarmInject prompts is not stated.
Supervised fine-tuning on ordinary or selected benign data. Only prompt injection into TTRL is tested.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
No test of what makes safety shallow.

missing.what: ASR before and after TTRL on AMC only (no injection), for 5 models × 3 jailbreak sets. Benign math adaptation leaves ASR mostly unchanged.
HarmInject built from the other source: Qwen-1.5B (Artifacts-built) shows no amplification; Llama-8B (JailbreakV-built) amplifies only transiently.
HarmInject bypasses the numeric-label reward filter for Qwen-0.5B/1.5B, so ASR still rises.

record.verdict_notes: The record's Artifacts rows r13-r15 (and r11's baseline) take values from Table 1, the no-injection run, instead of Table 2. I unlinked rows r1-r15 from V1: the injected data holds no harmful demonstrations, and the reward reinforces the model's own majority output. This is a different construct from harmful fine-tuning. All results are under TTRL with LoRA and no KL penalty, judged by LlamaGuard3-8B. No uncertainty is reported. Table 4's default post-TTRL accuracy for Llama-8B (11.0) differs from Table 3's (14.0).

versions.untested_parts: Does not test supervised fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples; tests harmful prompt injection during TTRL instead.
Tests benign instruction-following prompts injected into TTRL, not ordinary supervised fine-tuning or carefully selected benign fine-tuning data generally.
No per-token KL or response-position analysis.
No test of compliant prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as inference-time bypasses.
No weight or rank localization analysis.
No test of whether training data or objective produces first-token concentration or safety shallowness.
No training intended to spread safety across response positions or test of whether such training holds up.

relationships.condition: TTRL on attacker-built HarmInject prompts: Qwen-0.5B/1.5B (JailbreakV-28k-built) and Llama-3-8B (Artifacts-built), evaluated on held-out JailbreakV-28k
relationships.reason: The text reports significant harmfulness amplification for both Qwen models (r21, r22). Llama-8B ASR rose from about 1% to 45% (r23), though it stayed below full compliance.
relationships.display_finding: Harmfulness was significantly amplified for both Qwen models, and Llama-3-8B attack success rose from about 1% to 45%, short of full compliance.

relationships.condition: HarmInject built from the other source (Appendix C.6): Qwen-1.5B with Artifacts-built prompts; Llama-8B with JailbreakV-28k-built prompts
relationships.reason: From the text, not the rows. Qwen-1.5B showed no harmfulness amplification. Llama-8B rose only until step 100, then returned to its default rate. The effect depends on how the prompts are built.
relationships.display_finding: Qwen-1.5B showed no harmfulness amplification, and Llama-8B rose only until step 100 before returning to its default rate, so the effect depended on how the prompts were built.

relationships.condition: 50 UltraFeedback instruction-following prompts added to AMC TTRL: Qwen-0.5B, Llama-1B, Llama-3B
relationships.reason: ASR rose by +11, +13 and +16 percentage points on JailbreakV-28k (r16, r18, r19).
relationships.display_finding: Attack success on JailbreakV-28k rose by 11, 13 and 16 percentage points.

relationships.condition: Same UltraFeedback injection: Qwen-1.5B and Llama-8B
relationships.reason: ASR rose by only +3 and +2 percentage points (r17, r20).
relationships.display_finding: With UltraFeedback data injected, ASR rose by only 3 and 2 percentage points for Qwen-1.5B and Llama-8B.

relationships.condition: TTRL on benign AMC math prompts only (RQ1, Table 1)
relationships.reason: From the text, no row yet. ASR barely changed on three jailbreak sets for all five models (max +2). Llama-3B on WildJailbreak fell by 30. Benign math-only adaptation did not erode safety.
relationships.display_finding: ASR barely changed on three jailbreak sets for all five models (at most +2), and Llama-3B on WildJailbreak fell by 30.
